institutions.name: University of Oxford
institutions.summary: The oldest university in the English-speaking world, which grew up from schools of the late 11th and 12th centuries and expanded rapidly after 1167. A leading centre of scholastic philosophy, natural philosophy and theology (Grosseteste, Scotus, Ockham, Wyclif), it was the Anglican establishment's university from the Reformation until the religious tests were abolished in the 19th century.
institutions.notes: 1096 is the conventional date for the first evidence of teaching; organised studium dates from c.1167-1200. No founding charter exists.

institutions.name: University of Cambridge
institutions.summary: Founded by masters and students leaving Oxford in 1209, Cambridge became England's second university and received papal recognition as a studium generale in 1318. A centre of the English Reformation and later of mathematics and natural philosophy (Newton, Maxwell), it admitted women to examinations in the late 19th century.

institutions.name: University of Northampton (medieval)
institutions.summary: A short-lived studium formed by masters and students who left Cambridge (with Oxford sympathisers) in 1260-61. Licensed by Henry III, it was suppressed in 1265 after its scholars fought against the king and Oxford petitioned against a rival.
institutions.notes: Exact numbers and the degree of Oxford participation are uncertain.

institutions.name: Stamford secession
institutions.summary: A secession of mainly northern masters and students from Oxford, among them men of Brasenose Hall, who tried to set up a rival studium at Stamford. Edward III suppressed it in 1335; Oxford graduates swore never to lecture at Stamford until 1827.
institutions.notes: Its status as a true university is doubtful; classed here as an attempted studium.

institutions.name: Inns of Court
institutions.summary: Self-governing societies of common lawyers in London that from the 14th century trained students in English law through readings and moots. Called 'the third university of England', they never became a studium generale.
institutions.notes: Origins are obscure; Lincoln's Inn records begin in 1422, but the inns were active by the mid-14th century.

institutions.name: Royal College of Physicians of London
institutions.summary: Chartered by Henry VIII at Thomas Linacre's instance to license physicians in London. It sponsored anatomy lectures, notably the Lumleian lectures from 1582, at which William Harvey first taught the circulation of the blood.
institutions.notes: The college moved several times within London (Knightrider St, Amen Corner 1614, Warwick Lane 1674, Pall Mall East 1825); a single City location is given.

institutions.name: Gresham College
institutions.summary: Founded under Sir Thomas Gresham's will, it provided free public lectures in London by seven professors (divinity, astronomy, geometry, music, law, medicine, rhetoric). In the 17th century it was a hub of the new science and the Royal Society's first home.

institutions.name: Northampton Academy
institutions.summary: The leading Dissenting academy of the 18th century, run by Philip Doddridge, offering a broad curriculum in English for ministers and lay students excluded from the universities. After Doddridge's death it moved to Daventry and later back to Northampton.
institutions.notes: Opened at Market Harborough in mid-1729 and moved to Northampton in December 1729. After dissolution in 1798 the Coward Trust reopened it at Wymondley (1799).

institutions.name: Warrington Academy
institutions.summary: A rational Dissenting academy that offered a university-level education in classics, science and modern subjects to Nonconformists. Its tutors included Joseph Priestley and John Aikin; it closed in 1783 and was succeeded by Manchester Academy.

institutions.name: Manchester Academy
institutions.summary: Unitarian successor to Warrington Academy, it provided higher education for Dissenters and trained ministers. It moved repeatedly and settled in Oxford in 1889 (today Harris Manchester College).

institutions.name: New College, Hackney
institutions.summary: A short-lived rational Dissenting academy near London, offering a university curriculum. Associated with Richard Price and Joseph Priestley, it became notorious for radical sympathies during the French Revolution and collapsed financially.

institutions.name: Royal Military Academy, Woolwich
institutions.summary: Founded by royal warrant to train officers of the Royal Artillery and Royal Engineers in mathematics, fortification and gunnery. It was Britain's leading school of applied mathematics and science in the 18th century.

institutions.name: Royal Military College
institutions.summary: Officer-training college for the infantry and cavalry, founded on John Le Marchant's plans. Its senior department trained staff officers.
institutions.notes: The senior department began at High Wycombe in 1799; the college was formally established by royal warrant in 1802.

institutions.name: Royal Naval College, Greenwich
institutions.summary: Established in the former Greenwich Hospital to give naval officers advanced education in mathematics, physics, engineering and naval architecture.

institutions.name: Royal College of Science
institutions.summary: Began as the Royal College of Chemistry under A.W. Hofmann, Britain's first school of research chemistry, absorbed by the state science schools and reorganised as the Normal School of Science (1881) and Royal College of Science (1890). T.H. Huxley made it the main training ground for science teachers.

institutions.name: Royal School of Mines
alt: Metropolitan School of Science applied to Mining and the Arts
institutions.summary: State school of mining and geology founded with the Museum of Practical Geology in Jermyn Street. Huxley, Tyndall and Lyon Playfair taught there.

institutions.name: City and Guilds Central Technical College
institutions.summary: Engineering college founded by the City of London livery companies through the City and Guilds of London Institute. It trained engineers and technical teachers in South Kensington.

institutions.name: Royal Veterinary College
institutions.summary: The first veterinary school in Britain, founded by the Odiham Agricultural Society in Camden Town. It received a royal charter in 1875.

institutions.name: Royal Agricultural College
institutions.summary: The first agricultural college in the English-speaking world, founded by local landowners and chartered by Queen Victoria.

institutions.name: Royal Indian Engineering College
institutions.summary: Founded by the India Office to train civil engineers for the Public Works Department in India; it closed in 1906.

institutions.name: University College London
institutions.summary: Founded as 'London University' by Henry Brougham, Thomas Campbell and Dissenting and utilitarian supporters to provide university education without religious tests. It was the first English university institution to admit students regardless of religion and, from 1878, women on equal terms.

institutions.name: King's College London
institutions.summary: Founded by Anglicans, with the Duke of Wellington's support and a royal charter from George IV, as a Church of England response to the 'godless' London University. It developed strong science, engineering and medical teaching.

institutions.name: University of London
institutions.summary: Chartered as an examining and degree-granting body for University College, King's College and other affiliated institutions. Its external degrees (from 1858) and its admission of women to degrees (1878) made it the most open university in Britain.
institutions.notes: Location given as Somerset House; the university's offices moved to Burlington Gardens in 1870 and to the Imperial Institute in 1900. Bedford College (1849) was independent and is recorded here as an access event.

institutions.name: University of Durham
institutions.summary: Founded by the Dean and Chapter of Durham Cathedral and Bishop Van Mildert, with an Act of Parliament, as England's third university. Anglican in character, it later incorporated colleges of medicine and science in Newcastle.

institutions.name: Durham College of Science, Newcastle
institutions.summary: Science college founded by the University of Durham with the North of England Institute of Mining Engineers. Renamed Durham College of Science in 1883 and Armstrong College in 1904.

institutions.name: St David's College, Lampeter
institutions.summary: Founded by Bishop Thomas Burgess of St Davids to train Welsh Anglican clergy, it was the oldest degree-awarding institution in Wales.

institutions.name: Owens College
institutions.summary: Founded from the bequest of merchant John Owens, it became the leading English civic college and the first college of the Victoria University. It was strong in chemistry, physics and engineering.

institutions.name: Victoria University
institutions.summary: England's first civic federal university, chartered with Owens College as its first college and later joined by Liverpool and Leeds. It admitted women to degrees from the start and was dissolved into separate universities in 1903-04.

institutions.name: University College Liverpool
institutions.summary: Civic college founded by Liverpool citizens, which joined the Victoria University in 1884 and became the University of Liverpool in 1903.

institutions.name: Yorkshire College
institutions.summary: Founded as a college of science for Yorkshire's industries, it broadened into arts and medicine, joined the Victoria University in 1887 and became the University of Leeds in 1904.

institutions.name: Mason College
institutions.summary: Science college founded by industrialist Josiah Mason, it became Mason University College in 1897 and the University of Birmingham by royal charter in 1900.
institutions.notes: Foundation deed 1870 and foundation stone 1875; formal opening 1 October 1880.

institutions.name: University College Bristol
institutions.summary: Civic college that admitted women from its foundation; it became the University of Bristol in 1909.

institutions.name: Firth College
institutions.summary: Arts and science college founded by steel manufacturer Mark Firth; merged into University College Sheffield in 1897 and the University of Sheffield in 1905.

institutions.name: University College Nottingham
institutions.summary: Civic college founded by Nottingham corporation out of university-extension lectures; it prepared students for London degrees.

institutions.name: University College of Wales, Aberystwyth
institutions.summary: The first university college in Wales, funded largely by public subscription including 'the pennies of the poor'. A constituent of the University of Wales from 1893.

institutions.name: University College of South Wales and Monmouthshire
institutions.summary: University college founded after the Aberdare Report with Treasury support; a constituent of the University of Wales from 1893.

institutions.name: University College of North Wales, Bangor
institutions.summary: University college founded after the Aberdare Report; a constituent of the University of Wales from 1893.

institutions.name: University of Wales
institutions.summary: Federal degree-awarding university uniting the colleges at Aberystwyth, Bangor and Cardiff, which admitted women on equal terms from the start.
institutions.notes: A federal body without a single seat; the registry's location is nominal.

institutions.name: University of St Andrews
institutions.summary: Scotland's first university, founded by Bishop Henry Wardlaw and confirmed by Antipope Benedict XIII. It became a centre of the Scottish Reformation and was organised around the colleges of St Salvator, St Leonard and St Mary.
institutions.notes: Teaching began in 1410 and Wardlaw's charter dates from 1411; the papal bulls of 1413 are taken as founding.

institutions.name: University of Glasgow
institutions.summary: Founded by bull of Nicholas V at the request of Bishop William Turnbull and James II. Reorganised by Andrew Melville in 1577, it became a leading centre of the Scottish Enlightenment and of 19th-century physics and engineering.

institutions.name: King's College, Aberdeen
institutions.summary: Founded by Bishop William Elphinstone under a bull of Alexander VI, modelled on Paris and Orléans, with Hector Boece as first principal. It merged with Marischal College in 1860 to form the University of Aberdeen.

institutions.name: Marischal College
institutions.summary: Protestant university founded in the burgh of Aberdeen by George Keith, 5th Earl Marischal, as a rival to King's College. It merged with King's in 1860.

institutions.name: University of Aberdeen
institutions.summary: Formed under the Universities (Scotland) Act 1858 by uniting King's College and Marischal College.

institutions.name: University of Edinburgh
institutions.summary: Founded by the town council under a royal charter of James VI as a Protestant 'Tounis College'. Its medical school, established in 1726, made it a leading European centre of medicine and the Scottish Enlightenment.

institutions.name: University of Fraserburgh
institutions.summary: A college founded by Sir Alexander Fraser of Philorth under parliamentary charter. It functioned briefly under principal Charles Ferme and ended when he was imprisoned for attending the Aberdeen General Assembly.
institutions.notes: End date uncertain; teaching ceased c.1605.

institutions.name: University College Dundee
institutions.summary: Founded by Mary Ann Baxter, open to both sexes, and affiliated with St Andrews from 1897.

institutions.name: Anderson's Institution
alt: Glasgow and West of Scotland Technical College
institutions.summary: Founded under the will of natural philosopher John Anderson for 'useful learning', it pioneered science lectures for working men and women. It became the Glasgow and West of Scotland Technical College in 1887.

institutions.name: School of Arts of Edinburgh
institutions.summary: One of the first mechanics' institutes, founded by Leonard Horner to teach science to artisans. It became Heriot-Watt College in 1885.

institutions.name: Edinburgh Veterinary College
institutions.summary: Founded by William Dick, it became one of Britain's main veterinary schools.

institutions.name: New College, Edinburgh
institutions.summary: Theological college of the Free Church of Scotland founded after the Disruption of 1843, with Thomas Chalmers as first principal.

institutions.name: University of Dublin (medieval)
institutions.summary: A medieval university attached to St Patrick's Cathedral under a 1312 bull of Clement V, organised by Archbishop Alexander de Bicknor in 1320. It never flourished and faded away before the Reformation.
institutions.notes: End date is conjectural; it had ceased functioning by the dissolution of the cathedral chapter in 1547.

institutions.name: University of Drogheda
institutions.summary: A university authorised by the Irish Parliament on the model of Oxford, which appears never to have functioned effectively.
institutions.notes: No evidence of sustained teaching; end date conjectural.

institutions.name: Trinity College Dublin
alt: College of the Holy and Undivided Trinity
institutions.summary: Founded by charter of Elizabeth I on the site of All Hallows priory as the sole college of the University of Dublin, to educate a Protestant elite. It remained the Anglican university of Ireland until tests were abolished in 1873.

institutions.name: Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland
institutions.summary: Chartered by George III to regulate surgery in Ireland, it opened a school of surgery in 1789 and moved to St Stephen's Green in 1810. It admitted women to its licence in 1885.

institutions.name: St Patrick's College, Maynooth
institutions.summary: Catholic seminary founded by Act of the Irish Parliament, after the French Revolution closed Irish colleges on the Continent. It became the largest seminary in the world and was made a pontifical university in 1896.

institutions.name: Queen's College, Belfast
institutions.summary: One of three non-denominational Queen's Colleges established by Peel's government to provide higher education to Irish Catholics and Presbyterians. It became Queen's University of Belfast in 1908.

institutions.name: Queen's College, Cork
institutions.summary: Non-denominational Queen's College condemned by the Catholic hierarchy as 'godless'; George Boole was its first professor of mathematics.

institutions.name: Queen's College, Galway
institutions.summary: The western Queen's College, non-denominational and state-funded; it struggled for students owing to Catholic opposition.

institutions.name: Queen's University in Ireland
institutions.summary: Federal examining university for the three Queen's Colleges. It was dissolved in 1882 and replaced by the Royal University of Ireland.

institutions.name: Catholic University of Ireland
institutions.summary: Founded by the Irish Catholic bishops, with papal encouragement, as a Catholic alternative to Trinity and the Queen's Colleges, with John Henry Newman as first rector. Lacking a charter, it could not grant recognised degrees; its University College was run by the Jesuits from 1883.

institutions.name: Royal University of Ireland
institutions.summary: Examining university created by the University Education (Ireland) Act 1879 and chartered in 1880, open to candidates of any college or none. It awarded degrees to women from 1884 and was replaced by the National University in 1908.

institutions.name: Royal College of Science for Ireland
institutions.summary: State college of applied science on St Stephen's Green, developed from the Museum of Irish Industry, training engineers, chemists and science teachers.

institutions.name: Uppsala University
institutions.summary: Scandinavia's first university, founded by bull of Sixtus IV at the request of Archbishop Jakob Ulvsson. It collapsed during the Reformation but was refounded in 1595 and, endowed by Gustavus Adolphus, became the intellectual centre of Sweden's age of greatness and of Linnaean natural history.

institutions.name: Lund University
institutions.summary: Founded by Charles XI after Sweden acquired Scania, to integrate the province culturally. Closed during the Scanian War, it reopened in 1682 and became Sweden's second university.

institutions.name: Karolinska Institute
institutions.summary: Founded by Charles XIII to train army surgeons after the high medical losses of the Finnish War. It became a leading medical school, with Berzelius among its early professors.

institutions.name: Royal Institute of Technology
institutions.summary: Sweden's main technical school, founded as the Technological Institute and renamed the Royal Institute of Technology in 1877.

institutions.name: Chalmers Institute
institutions.summary: Founded with the bequest of William Chalmers, director of the Swedish East India Company, as an industrial school; it developed into a technical college.

institutions.name: Falun Mining School
institutions.summary: Sweden's school of mining at the Great Copper Mountain; its higher course moved to KTH in 1869.

institutions.name: Karlberg Military Academy
institutions.summary: Swedish officer-training academy in Karlberg Palace.

institutions.name: Stockholm University College
institutions.summary: A privately and municipally funded institution for free research and public lectures, without the conservative traditions of Uppsala and Lund. Sofia Kovalevskaya became its professor of mathematics.

institutions.name: Gothenburg University College
institutions.summary: Founded through donations by Gothenburg citizens, initially teaching humanities. It became a full university in 1954.

institutions.name: University of Copenhagen
institutions.summary: Founded by Christian I under a 1475 bull of Sixtus IV, it lapsed during the Reformation and was refounded in 1537 as a Lutheran university. It was the sole university of Denmark-Norway until 1811.

institutions.name: Polytechnic College
institutions.summary: Denmark's polytechnic, founded on H.C. Ørsted's initiative to teach applied natural science, with Ørsted as director until 1850.

institutions.name: Royal Veterinary School
institutions.summary: Founded by Peter Christian Abildgaard, one of the first veterinary schools in Europe. It merged into the Royal Veterinary and Agricultural College in 1856.

institutions.name: Royal Veterinary and Agricultural College
institutions.summary: Danish college of veterinary science, agriculture and forestry.

institutions.name: Sorø Academy
institutions.summary: Knightly academy founded by Christian IV in the former Cistercian abbey to educate the nobility, briefly a rival to the university. Closed and revived several times, it became a school in 1822.

institutions.name: Royal Frederick University
institutions.summary: Norway's first university, founded by Frederick VI after long Norwegian demands. It trained the officials of the independent Norway after 1814.

institutions.name: Kongsberg Mining Seminary
institutions.summary: Mining academy at the Kongsberg silver mines, one of the earliest in Europe. Its teaching moved to the new university in Christiania.

institutions.name: Norwegian Military Academy
institutions.summary: Officer and military-engineering school, which also educated Norway's first civil engineers and surveyors.

institutions.name: Bessastaðir School
institutions.summary: Iceland's sole learned school in the early 19th century, successor to the cathedral schools of Skálholt and Hólar. It trained the generation of the Icelandic national revival before moving to Reykjavík.

institutions.name: Pastoral Seminary of Reykjavík
institutions.summary: Iceland's first institution of higher education, training Lutheran clergy; it merged into the University of Iceland in 1911.

institutions.name: Reykjavík Medical School
institutions.summary: Medical school for training Icelandic physicians; it merged into the University of Iceland in 1911.

institutions.name: Royal Academy of Turku / Imperial Alexander University
institutions.summary: Founded in Åbo during Queen Christina's minority on the initiative of Governor-General Per Brahe, it was Finland's only university. After the 1827 Turku fire it was moved to the new capital, Helsinki, as the Imperial Alexander University, where it nurtured the Finnish national movement.

institutions.name: Helsinki Polytechnic
institutions.summary: Finland's technical school, which became the Polytechnic Institute in 1879 and the Helsinki University of Technology in 1908.

events.title: Earliest teaching at Oxford
events.desc: Conventional date for the first recorded teaching in Oxford; the studium grew up spontaneously around the town's churches and religious houses.

events.title: English scholars recalled from Paris
events.desc: Henry II's quarrel with Becket and ban on English clerks studying in Paris brought many masters and students to Oxford, turning it into a studium generale.

events.title: Dispersal of 1209
events.desc: After townsmen hanged two or three clerks in reprisal for a killing, the masters suspended teaching and dispersed; some went to Reading and others to Cambridge, founding the studium there.

events.title: Legatine ordinance
events.desc: The papal legate Nicholas of Tusculum restored the studium, imposing penance and payments on the town and providing for a chancellor, the first formal recognition of the university.

events.title: St Scholastica Day riot
events.desc: A tavern brawl on 10 February escalated into three days of fighting in which some 63 scholars were killed and halls sacked; the town was subjected to an annual penance and the university given control over much of town life.

events.title: Suppression of Lollardy
events.desc: Archbishop Arundel's visitation enforced his 1409 Constitutions against Wycliffite teaching, ending Oxford's role as a centre of Lollard thought.

events.title: Henrician Reformation injunctions
events.desc: Thomas Cromwell's royal visitation abolished the teaching of canon law and scholastic commentaries and imposed the royal supremacy; Regius chairs followed in 1546 and Christ Church was refounded the same year.

events.title: Act of Incorporation
events.desc: Parliament incorporated the university and confirmed its privileges; from 1581 subscription to the Thirty-Nine Articles was required at matriculation, excluding Catholics and Dissenters.

events.title: Laudian Code
events.desc: Chancellor William Laud's statutes codified the university's constitution and curriculum, which remained in force until the 19th-century reforms.

events.title: Oxford University Act
events.desc: The Act reformed governance and abolished religious tests at matriculation and for the BA, opening the university to Dissenters as undergraduates.

events.title: Universities Tests Act
events.desc: Abolished religious tests for most degrees, fellowships and offices at Oxford, Cambridge and Durham (except divinity).

events.title: First women's halls
events.desc: Lady Margaret Hall and Somerville Hall opened for women students, who could attend lectures and from 1884 sit some university examinations, though they could not take degrees until 1920.

events.title: Scholars from Oxford settle at Cambridge
events.desc: Masters fleeing the Oxford suspendium of 1209 began teaching in Cambridge, where a studium survived after most returned to Oxford in 1214.

events.title: Influx from Paris
events.desc: During the Paris strike of 1229-31 Henry III invited the dispersing masters to England, and many settled at Cambridge (and Oxford).

events.title: Royal writs of Henry III
events.desc: Henry III's writs placed scholars under the chancellor's jurisdiction and regulated lodging rents, the first royal protection of the university.

events.title: Papal recognition
events.desc: Pope John XXII's bull confirmed Cambridge as a studium generale.

events.title: Peasants' Revolt
events.desc: Townspeople allied with the rebels sacked Corpus Christi College and burnt university charters and records on Market Hill.

events.title: Henrician injunctions
events.desc: The royal injunctions abolished canon law degrees and imposed the royal supremacy; Cambridge became a seedbed of English Protestantism and Trinity College was founded in 1546.

events.title: Elizabethan statutes
events.desc: New statutes concentrated power in the heads of houses, shaping the university's constitution until the 19th century; the university was incorporated by Act of Parliament in 1571.

events.title: Cambridge University Act
events.desc: Removed religious tests for matriculation and bachelor's degrees, admitting Dissenters as graduates.

events.title: College for women at Hitchin
events.desc: Emily Davies opened a college for women at Hitchin, which moved to Girton in 1873 and prepared women for Cambridge examinations.

events.title: Universities Tests Act
events.desc: Abolished religious tests for most degrees and posts, completing the opening of Cambridge to non-Anglicans.

events.title: Newnham lectures
events.desc: Anne Clough's house for women attending lectures opened; it became Newnham College in 1880.

events.title: Women admitted to the Tripos
events.desc: Grace of 1881 formally admitted women from Girton and Newnham to the Tripos examinations, though not to degrees.

events.title: Royal licence for the Northampton studium
events.desc: Henry III permitted seceding masters from Cambridge to establish a university at Northampton.

events.title: Siege of Northampton
events.desc: Students fought on the baronial side when Henry III stormed the town in April 1264.

events.title: Royal dissolution
events.desc: Henry III ordered the studium dissolved, citing harm to Oxford; the scholars returned to Oxford and Cambridge.

events.title: Oxford secession to Stamford
events.desc: Masters and students left Oxford after factional disputes and began teaching at Stamford.

events.title: Suppressed by Edward III
events.desc: The king ordered the scholars back to Oxford and the studium was broken up.

events.title: Emergence of the inns
events.desc: Societies of apprentices at law took up residence in hostels between the City and Westminster, forming the four inns.

events.title: Council of Legal Education
events.desc: The four inns established a joint Council of Legal Education with lectures and examinations for the Bar, compulsory from 1872.

events.title: Royal charter
events.desc: Henry VIII's letters patent incorporated the College of Physicians at Linacre's petition.

events.title: Lumleian lectures
events.desc: Lord Lumley and Richard Caldwell endowed surgical/anatomical lectures given at the college.

events.title: First lectures
events.desc: Lectures began in Gresham's mansion in Bishopsgate, administered by the City and the Mercers' Company.

events.title: Royal Society founded at Gresham
events.desc: After a lecture by Christopher Wren in November 1660, the group that became the Royal Society was formed and met at Gresham College until 1710.

events.title: Gresham House demolished
events.desc: The mansion was sold to the Crown and demolished, and the lectures moved to a room over the Royal Exchange.

events.title: New college building
events.desc: A purpose-built Gresham College opened on Gresham Street.

events.title: Doddridge opens his academy
events.desc: Philip Doddridge began teaching at Market Harborough and moved the academy to Northampton at the end of 1729.

events.title: Move to Daventry
events.desc: Under Caleb Ashworth the academy moved to Daventry, where Joseph Priestley studied (1752-55).

events.title: Return to Northampton
events.desc: The academy returned to Northampton under John Horsey.

events.title: Dissolved by the Coward Trustees
events.desc: Concerned at heterodox teaching, the trustees closed the academy; its successor opened at Wymondley in 1799.

events.title: Academy opened
events.desc: Opened by Lancashire and Cheshire Dissenters under John Seddon with John Taylor as divinity tutor.

events.title: Closure
events.desc: Financial difficulties and indiscipline led to closure; its library and ethos passed to Manchester Academy (1786).

events.title: Manchester Academy opened
events.desc: Founded by Manchester Dissenters as successor to Warrington Academy.

events.title: Move to York
events.desc: The academy moved to York under Charles Wellbeloved.

events.title: Return to Manchester
events.desc: Returned to Manchester as Manchester New College, affiliated to the University of London.

events.title: Move to London
events.desc: Moved to University Hall, Gordon Square, near University College.

events.title: Move to Oxford
events.desc: Settled in Oxford as Manchester College, opening new buildings in 1893.

events.title: College opened
events.desc: Opened by London Dissenters as a university-level academy for ministers and laymen.

events.title: Closure
events.desc: Debts and suspicion of political radicalism forced closure.

events.title: Royal warrant
events.desc: George II's warrant established the academy within the Royal Arsenal.

events.title: New buildings on Woolwich Common
events.desc: The academy moved into James Wyatt's buildings on Woolwich Common.

events.title: Royal warrant
events.desc: Royal Military College established with its junior department at Great Marlow.

events.title: Move to Sandhurst
events.desc: The college moved into new buildings at Sandhurst, Berkshire.

events.title: College opened
events.desc: Admiralty order in council created the college, which absorbed the Royal Naval College at Portsmouth.

events.title: Royal College of Chemistry opened
events.desc: Founded by subscription with Prince Albert's patronage, with A.W. Hofmann as professor, in Oxford Street.

events.title: Taken over by the state
events.desc: The College of Chemistry was absorbed into the government's Metropolitan School of Science applied to Mining and the Arts.

events.title: Move to South Kensington
events.desc: Chemistry and biology teaching moved into new buildings in South Kensington.

events.title: Normal School of Science
events.desc: Reorganised under Huxley as the Normal School of Science for training teachers; renamed Royal College of Science in 1890.

events.title: Government School of Mines opened
events.desc: Opened with the Museum of Practical Geology under Henry De la Beche.

events.title: Renamed Royal School of Mines
events.desc: The school took its permanent name and focused on mining and metallurgy.

events.title: Central Institution opened
events.desc: Opened in Alfred Waterhouse's building in Exhibition Road.

events.title: College opened
events.desc: Founded with Charles Vial de Sainbel, trained at Lyon, as first professor.

events.title: Royal charter
events.desc: Granted a royal charter as the Royal Veterinary College.

events.title: Royal charter
events.desc: Founded with a royal charter and opened to students in 1846.

events.title: College opened
events.desc: Opened at Coopers Hill near Egham under the Secretary of State for India.

events.title: Deed of settlement
events.desc: London University was established as a joint-stock company; teaching began in Gower Street in October 1828.

events.title: Chartered as University College
events.desc: Denied degree-granting powers, it was incorporated as University College, one of the two colleges of the new University of London.

events.title: Women admitted to classes
events.desc: Following the University of London's admission of women to degrees, UCL opened most of its classes to women.

events.title: Royal charter
events.desc: George IV's charter founded the college; teaching began in the Strand in October 1831.

events.title: College of the University of London
events.desc: Became one of the two original colleges of the University of London.

events.title: Royal charter
events.desc: William IV's charter created the University of London as an examining body for UCL and King's.

events.title: Bedford College for women
events.desc: Elizabeth Jesser Reid founded the Ladies' College in Bedford Square, the first higher-education college for women in Britain; its students later took London degrees.

events.title: External degrees
events.desc: A new charter opened degrees to candidates regardless of where they had studied.

events.title: Women admitted to degrees
events.desc: A supplemental charter made London the first British university to admit women to its degrees; the first four women graduated BA in 1880.

events.title: University of London Act

events.desc: Specialised professorships replaced regents who taught every subject, a model for Enlightenment teaching.
